nodes.title: Spectral theory of unbounded operators
nodes.abstract:
The measured values of an observable are the points of the spectrum of the operator representing it,
so the spectral theory of an unbounded operator is what connects the formalism to experiment. For
partially defined operators on a complex Hilbert space it comprises the resolvent and the resolvent
set, the spectrum with its point, residual and continuous parts, the regularity domain with the
deficiency subspace and the defect number, the numerical range, and spectral measures. Two results
carry the physical content: for a symmetric operator every point off the real axis is a point of
regularity, and the defect numbers at i and -i decide essential self-adjointness; for a self-adjoint
operator the spectrum is real and the residual spectrum empty, so a measurement returns a real
number. The algebraic theory of the operators themselves lives in the operator algebra.

subsections.title: Resolvent and spectrum
subsections.body:
A complex number z lies in the resolvent set of an operator T {1} when T - z has a bounded inverse,
the resolvent; the resolvent set is open, and for a closed operator it is exactly the set of z for
which T - z is a bijection from the domain onto the space. [1] The spectrum is the complement of the
resolvent set; it is closed, and splits into the point, residual and continuous spectra. [2]
Resolvents satisfy the two resolvent identities, relating resolvents at two points and of two
operators. [3] The treatment follows the standard references of Hall {2}, Reed and Simon {3}, and
Schmüdgen {4}.

subsections.title: Regularity domain and numerical range
subsections.body:
A point z is a point of regularity when T - z is bounded below. The regularity domain is open, the
deficiency subspace at z is the orthogonal complement of the range of T - z, and its dimension is
the defect number; for a closable operator it is constant on each connected component of the
regularity domain. [4] The numerical range is the set of values of the pairing of a unit vector with
its image; it is convex by the Toeplitz-Hausdorff theorem, and the exterior of its closure consists
of points of regularity. [5]

subsections.title: Symmetric operators
subsections.body:
The numerical range of a symmetric operator is real, and so is described by its projection to the
real axis. [6] Every point off the real axis is therefore a point of regularity, and the regularity
domain is connected when the operator is bounded above or below. [7] A symmetric operator whose
defect numbers at i and -i both vanish is essentially self-adjoint. [8] The eigenvalues of a
symmetric operator are real. [9]

subsections.title: Self-adjoint operators
subsections.body:
For a self-adjoint operator the resolvent set and the regularity domain coincide, and every complex
number with non-zero imaginary part lies in the resolvent set, with T - z onto. [10] The spectrum of
a self-adjoint operator lies in the real axis and its residual spectrum is empty. [11] Conjugation
by a unitary preserves self-adjointness, so an observable keeps its status under a change of
representation. [12]

subsections.title: Spectral measures and the spectral theorem
subsections.body:
A spectral measure is a vector measure valued in the bounded operators whose values are star
projections and which sends the whole outcome space to the identity. [13] The projections of two
measurable sets compose to the projection of their intersection, disjoint sets give orthogonal
projections, and all of them commute. [14]

Every self-adjoint operator is the integral of the identity against a spectral measure supported on
its spectrum; equivalently, it is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by a real function on an L²
space. [TODO] The spectral theorem yields a functional calculus, and Stone's theorem gives the
unitary time evolution generated by a self-adjoint Hamiltonian. [TODO] The spectrum of a
multiplication operator is the essential range of its multiplier. [TODO]

nodes.title: QuantumSystem
nodes.abstract:
A quantum system in non-relativistic quantum mechanics is fixed by two choices: a complex
Hilbert space, and a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator on it. Everything else is built from that
pair: the trivial system on the zero-dimensional space, unitary equivalence of systems, the sum
of two systems, and the dynamics, namely the Schrödinger equation, the time evolution operator,
the energy eigenvalues and eigenbases, and the passage to the Heisenberg picture.

content.heading: Content (Alpha)
content.intro:
A quantum system consists of a complete complex inner-product space together with a
self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator on it. [1] The trivial, zero-dimensional Hilbert space carries
a unique quantum system, the zero system. [2] Two systems are unitarily equivalent when some
unitary map between their Hilbert spaces carries one Hamiltonian to the other by conjugation, and
unitary equivalence is an equivalence relation on quantum systems. [3] Two quantum systems add,
giving the system on the product of their Hilbert spaces whose Hamiltonian is, schematically, the
sum of theirs. [TODO]

The dynamics of a quantum system is governed by its Hamiltonian. The Schrödinger equation is an
equation for a wavefunction depending on time and valued in the domain of the Hamiltonian.
[TODO] The time evolution operator is a bounded operator on the Hilbert space for each time.
[TODO] The Hamiltonian has energy eigenspaces, eigenvectors and eigenvalues [TODO], and a
system may admit an energy eigenbasis. [TODO] Conjugation with the time evolution operator
moves an operator into and out of the Heisenberg picture. [TODO]

declarations.doc: A quantum system is identified by its Hilbert space and self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator.
declarations.signature:
structure QuantumSystem where
  HS : Type*
  [instNormed : NormedAddCommGroup HS]
  [instInner : InnerProductSpace ℂ HS]
  [instComplete : CompleteSpace HS]
  ℋ : HS →ₗ.[ℂ] HS
  ℋ_self_adjoint : IsSelfAdjoint ℋ

nodes.title: Qubits
nodes.abstract:
A qubit is a two-level quantum system, labelled by the two-element type of its computational basis.
A pure state of a qubit is a ket on that type, and a general state is a density matrix on it, both
coming from the theory of finite dimensional systems. What is specific to qubits is the standard
single-qubit gates, the controlled version of a unitary with a qubit as control, the Bloch sphere
with its angular parameterization and the geometric phase of triples of states, and, for pairs and
registers of qubits, entanglement and universality.

subsections.title: States
subsections.body:
A qubit {1} is labelled by the two-element type indexing its computational basis. [1] Its pure
states are kets of a finite dimensional system: functions on the basis normalized to unit length, with dual
bras, the bra-ket pairing, the normalization condition in both its componentwise and its
inner-product form, the computational basis states and the uniform superposition. [2] The product of
two systems carries product and entangled kets and the maximally entangled state, so that Bell-type
states of a pair of qubits can be written. [6] Two kets that differ by a unit complex number
represent the same physical state, and the quotient by this relation gives states up to a global
phase. [7]

subsections.title: Gates
subsections.body:
The standard single-qubit gates are the three Pauli gates, the Hadamard gate and the two phase
gates, each an element of the unitary group on a qubit. [3] Each squares to a known gate, the three
Pauli gates anticommute, the phase gates commute with the Pauli gate they are built from and with
each other, and conjugation by the Hadamard gate exchanges two of the Pauli gates. [4] A unitary on
an arbitrary register has a controlled version with a qubit as control; it acts as the unitary on
the block where the control is one, the controlled-NOT gate is the controlled Pauli X gate with its
familiar matrix, controlled gates compose as their targets do, and conjugating the control by a
Pauli gate has an explicit effect. [5]

The rotation gates about the three coordinate axes, together with a phase, decompose an arbitrary
single-qubit unitary, and conjugation by a single-qubit unitary is a rotation of the Bloch sphere.
[TODO]

subsections.title: The Bloch sphere and geometric phase
subsections.body:
The Bloch sphere is the unit sphere of three-dimensional Euclidean space, parameterized by a polar
and an azimuthal angle, and the dot product of two of its points is given in terms of those angles.
[8] A geodesic triangle on the Bloch sphere has a solid angle, and three pure states have a
Bargmann invariant, whose phase is invariant under cyclic permutation and negated under reversal of
the order, as an equation of angles, and whose norm is at most one. [9][10] This phase is
the geometric phase of Pancharatnam {2} and Berry {3}.

The Bloch vector of a state of a qubit is the triple of expectation values of the Pauli gates, and
it is a bijection from states onto the closed unit ball of three-dimensional Euclidean space.
[TODO] It restricts to a bijection from pure states up to a global phase onto the Bloch sphere,
so that the angular parameterization presents the pure state with the given polar and azimuthal
angles. [TODO] Every state of a qubit is one half of the identity plus a real combination of the
Pauli gates, and the identity together with the three Pauli gates is a basis of the self-adjoint two
by two complex matrices. [TODO]

subsections.title: Measurement and distinguishability
subsections.body:
Measuring a qubit in the computational basis gives the two outcomes with probabilities, by the Born
rule, equal to the squared norms of the components of the state. [TODO] The fidelity of two
states of a qubit has a closed form in terms of their traces and determinants. [TODO]

subsections.title: Pairs and registers of qubits
subsections.body:
The Bell basis of the states of a pair of qubits is orthonormal, and the standard gates have an
explicit action on it. [TODO] The singlet and triplet states of a pair of qubits split their
state space into an antisymmetric line and a symmetric plane. [TODO] The positive partial
transpose test is complete for a pair of qubits: such a state is separable exactly when its partial
transpose is positive semidefinite. [TODO]

The state space of a register of several qubits is an iterated product, and a single-qubit gate
extends to a gate acting on one component of a register. [TODO] The Hadamard gate, one phase gate
and the controlled-NOT gate generate a dense subgroup of the special unitary group of a register, so
that they are universal for quantum computation. [TODO] Kets on a qubit are the unit vectors of
the finite dimensional Hilbert space of a two-element type. [TODO]

nodes.title: Dirac Fermions
nodes.abstract:
A Dirac fermion is the four-component spinor built from a left-handed Weyl fermion together with a
dual right-handed one: it is a complex vector space with a four-element chiral basis, carrying the
representation of SL(2, ℂ) induced from its two Weyl factors, and so of the Lorentz group through
its double cover. The gamma endomorphisms act in the chiral basis and satisfy the Clifford relations
for the Minkowski signature (+,−,−,−); their chirality operator gives complementary left and right
chiral projectors, and a change of coordinates turns them into the concrete gamma matrices of the
Dirac representation, which generate the Dirac algebra and realize it as a quotient of the Clifford
algebra of the Minkowski quadratic form. This is the setting for the Dirac equation, the Dirac
bilinears and the fermionic terms of the Standard Model Lagrangian.

subsections.title: Dirac spinors
subsections.body:
A Dirac fermion is a pair consisting of a left-handed Weyl fermion and a dual right-handed Weyl
fermion {1}. [1] Dirac fermions form a complex vector space, with addition and scalar
multiplication acting on the two Weyl components. [2] Decomposing a Dirac fermion into its Weyl
components is a complex linear equivalence. [3] The space has a four-element chiral basis, whose
elements are the basis elements of the two Weyl components. [4] SL(2, ℂ), the double cover of the
Lorentz group {2}, acts on Dirac fermions componentwise on the two Weyl factors. [5] This
representation is equivalent to the product of the representations on the Weyl components. [6]
The two-component treatment of Dirac fermions follows Dreiner, Haber and Martin {3}.

subsections.title: Gamma endomorphisms and chirality
subsections.body:
Clifford multiplication is a real linear map from Lorentz vectors to complex linear
endomorphisms of the Dirac fermions, written in the chiral basis with the library's Pauli-matrix
conventions; on the Lorentz basis it gives the upper-index gamma components γ^μ. [12] For any two
Lorentz vectors v and w, the anticommutator of their Clifford products is 2⟨v, w⟩ times the
identity, where ⟨v, w⟩ is the Minkowski product; the component relations
{γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2η^{μν}, the squares of the γ^μ and the anticommutation of distinct γ^μ follow, in
the signature (+,−,−,−). [13]

The chirality endomorphism γ⁵ has chiral matrix diag(−1,−1,1,1), squares to the identity, and
anticommutes with every gamma endomorphism. [14] The left and right chiral projectors
(1 − γ⁵)/2 and (1 + γ⁵)/2 have the corresponding diagonal matrices, are idempotent and mutually
orthogonal, and sum to the identity. [15] The chiral projectors are Lorentz equivariant.
[TODO]

subsections.title: The Dirac representation
subsections.body:
An algebra equivalence converts endomorphisms of the Dirac fermions into 4 × 4 matrices in the
Dirac representation, with an explicit change-of-coordinates formula from the chiral basis. [16]
Under it the gamma endomorphisms become the gamma matrices γ⁰, γ¹, γ², γ³ of the Dirac
representation, alongside the chirality matrix γ⁵ and the set the gamma matrices form. [7] These
matrices satisfy the Clifford anticommutator against the Minkowski metric in the signature
(+,−,−,−). [8]

The Dirac slash k̸ of a Lorentz vector k is its Clifford multiplication in the Dirac
representation, contracting the lowered coordinates of k with the gamma matrices. [9] It is real
linear in k, and extends to ordered products of slash factors. [9]

The Dirac algebra is the real subalgebra generated by the Dirac representations of the gamma
endomorphisms, and it contains each generator. [10] The Minkowski quadratic form induces an
algebra map from its Clifford algebra onto the Dirac algebra, and this map is surjective. [11]
The map is an isomorphism, its injectivity resting on dimension theory. [TODO]

subsections.title: Bilinears and field equations
subsections.body:
A Dirac fermion ψ has a Dirac adjoint ψ̄. [TODO] The Dirac bilinears ψ̄Γψ have definite
transformation behaviour under SL(2, ℂ). [TODO] A spinor field on spacetime is subject to the
Dirac equation. [TODO] A Dirac fermion has a charge conjugate, and the Majorana condition
identifies a fermion with its charge conjugate. [TODO]

nodes.title: Weyl Fermions
nodes.abstract:
Weyl fermions are the two-component spinors carrying the fundamental representations of SL(2, ℂ),
the double cover of the restricted Lorentz group. There are four of them — the left-handed and
right-handed Weyl spinors and their duals — each a complex vector space with a two-element basis and
a representation of SL(2, ℂ); on top of these sit the invariant contractions pairing each type with
its dual, the epsilon metrics that raise and lower spinor indices, the units realizing the duality,
and the identification of pairwise tensor products with 2 × 2 matrices. They underlie the Dirac
fermions and the fermionic sector of the Standard Model.

subsections.title: The four spinor spaces
subsections.body:
A left-handed Weyl spinor ψ_α is an element of a two-dimensional complex vector space. [1] A
right-handed Weyl spinor ψ^{α̇} is likewise an element of a two-dimensional complex vector space.
[2] Each has a dual, ψ^α and ψ_{α̇}, again a complex vector space. [3][4] Each of the four spaces
has a two-element basis, and every spinor expands in it. [5][6][7][8] Each carries a representation
of SL(2, ℂ), the double cover of the restricted Lorentz group {1}, whose matrix in that basis is the
defining matrix, its conjugate, its inverse transpose or its inverse conjugate transpose as
appropriate. [9][10][11][12] Each of these representations is irreducible, and Schur's lemma
holds for it: an endomorphism commuting with the representation is a scalar multiple of the
identity. [23][24][25][26] Weyl fermions are the building blocks of Dirac fermions {2}, and the
two-component formalism follows Dreiner, Haber and Martin {3}.

subsections.title: Contractions, metrics and units
subsections.body:
Each Weyl type pairs invariantly with its dual, giving bilinear maps that are also intertwining
maps of representations. [13] On basis elements these contractions are Kronecker deltas, and
each is symmetric under exchanging its two factors. [14]

The epsilon metrics ε_{αβ}, ε^{αβ}, ε_{α̇β̇} and ε^{α̇β̇} are invariant tensors, intertwining
maps out of the trivial representation, with explicit expansions in the basis. [15] Their
invariance rests on the raw epsilon matrix ε intertwining M ∈ SL(2, ℂ) with its inverse transpose,
Mε = ε(M⁻¹)ᵀ, and the complex conjugate of M with its inverse conjugate transpose. [16]
Contracting a metric with the metric of the dual type over one index gives the unit,
ε_{αβ}ε^{βγ} = δ_α^γ, and likewise for the other types. [17]

The units δ_α^β and δ^{α̇}_{β̇} realize the duality between each type and its dual, and
contracting a unit with a spinor returns that spinor. [18] Each unit is symmetric under exchange
of its two factors. [19]

subsections.title: Duality and matrices
subsections.body:
The dual of the left-handed representation is the representation on the dual left-handed
spinors. [20] The dual of the right-handed representation is the representation on the dual
right-handed spinors, equivariantly for SL(2, ℂ). [22][TODO] Pairwise tensor products of the
Weyl types are 2 × 2 complex matrices, equivariantly for the action of SL(2, ℂ). [21] The
right-handed representation is the complex conjugate of the left-handed one. [TODO]

subsections.title: Field equations
subsections.body:
A massless spinor field obeys the Weyl equation. [TODO] The Majorana condition relates a
left-handed Weyl fermion to a right-handed one. [TODO]

nodes.title: Lorentz Group
nodes.abstract:
The Lorentz group is the group of real matrices Λ preserving the Minkowski metric η, those
satisfying Λ * dual Λ = 1 where dual Λ = η Λᵀ η. It is the symmetry group of Minkowski spacetime,
and is used throughout the library: Lorentz tensors, Weyl and Dirac fermions, and the
electromagnetic potential are all characterized by how they transform under it. The group sits as a
closed subgroup of the general linear group, contains the boosts and the rotations, admits several
equivalent membership conditions, and has distinguished subsets: the proper transformations, the
orthochronous ones, and the restricted Lorentz group where both conditions hold.

subsections.title: The group
subsections.body:
A Lorentz transformation is a matrix Λ satisfying Λ * dual Λ = 1, where the dual is taken with
respect to the Minkowski matrix. [1] The Lorentz transformations form a group under matrix
multiplication. [2] Equivalently, Λ is Lorentz exactly when dual Λ * Λ = 1, when its transpose
is Lorentz, when −Λ is Lorentz, or when Λᵀ η Λ = η. [6] The Lorentz group embeds as a closed
subgroup of the general linear group, by a closed embedding. [3] It is a Lie group, by Cartan's
closed subgroup theorem. [TODO] It is the symmetry group of Minkowski spacetime {1}, and Lorentz
tensors {2}, Weyl fermions {3} and Dirac fermions {4} are characterized by how they transform under
it. A standard introduction is Jaffe {5}.

subsections.title: Boosts and rotations
subsections.body:
Every boost is a Lorentz transformation. [4] Every rotation of space is a Lorentz
transformation. [5] Every member of the restricted Lorentz group is a boost composed with a
rotation. [10]

subsections.title: Proper, orthochronous and restricted transformations
subsections.body:
A Lorentz transformation is proper when its determinant is 1. [7] It is orthochronous when it
preserves the direction of time, its time-time component being non-negative. [8] The restricted
Lorentz group consists of the transformations that are both proper and orthochronous. [9] The
orthochronous Lorentz transformations are characterized topologically within the Lorentz group.
[TODO]

nodes.title: Tensors
nodes.abstract:
A tensor species packages everything needed to work with a type of tensor in index notation — a
symmetry group, index colors with a representation and a basis for each, a dual-color involution,
and contraction, unit and metric data — and for each list of colors there are the tensors with those
indices, the pure tensors and the component labels. On this base rest the operations of ordinary
index notation: permutation and reindexing, tensor products, contraction within one tensor and
across two, evaluation of an index, raising and lowering against the metric, and conjugation, with
an elaborator turning pen-and-paper index expressions into these operations. Two species are built:
the real Lorentz tensors over the Lorentz group, supporting Lorentz vectors and covectors, the
Minkowski product, causal character, velocities and the rank-four Levi-Civita tensor; and the
complex Lorentz tensors over SL(2, ℂ), which add the Weyl fermion colors. A canonical equivariant
semilinear map takes the first species into the second.

subsections.title: Tensor species
subsections.body:
A tensor species consists of a symmetry group, a type of index colors, a representation and a
basis for each color, an involution sending each color to the dual color it may contract with,
and contraction and unit data satisfying coherence conditions. [1] A species may carry a metric:
an invariant tensor for each color whose contraction against the metric of the dual color is the
unit, this condition forming a class of its own. [2] The conditions defining a species also relate
the metrics to the basis vectors. [TODO]

subsections.title: Tensors and their components
subsections.body:
Given a species and a list of colors, the tensors with those indices form the tensor product of
the color representations over the index set, and the pure tensors are the choices of one vector
for each index. [3] A component label assigns a basis index to each tensor index. [4] A
component label of a single index is a basis index of its color, a label of a concatenated index
list is a pair of labels, and a label drops a contracted pair of indices. [5][6][7] A tensor
corresponds to its components in the component basis, and the tensors with no indices are the
scalars. [3]

subsections.title: Group action and reindexing
subsections.body:
The symmetry group acts on pure tensors and on tensors. [8] Indices permute along a
color-preserving map, equivariantly, functorially and injectively. [8] The maps that count as
reindexings are characterized and are closed under inverse and composition; they include the
index maps used by products, evaluation and contraction. [9]

subsections.title: Products
subsections.body:
The tensor product of two pure tensors, or of two tensors, concatenates their index lists. [10]
It has explicit components in the basis, is equivariant, and is compatible with swapping the
factors, permuting either factor, and rebracketing. [10]

subsections.title: Contraction
subsections.body:
A pair of indices of dual color contracts, on pure tensors and on tensors, deleting the pair from
the index list. [11][12][13] Contraction is equivariant, commutes with permutations, is symmetric
in the contracted pair, and contractions of two different pairs commute. [13] Its components in
the basis are sums over the contracted label. [14] Contracting inside one factor of a product
agrees with contracting the product. [15]

One tensor also contracts against another at an addressed slot, either with the result placed at
the end [16] or with the result placed at the slot. [17] For real Lorentz tensors the
result-to-end contraction has explicit components in the standard basis. [18]

subsections.title: Units, metrics, raising and lowering
subsections.body:
The unit tensor of a color is invariant under the group action, has explicit components, and is
the permuted unit tensor of the dual color. [19] The metric tensor of a color is invariant, and
contracting it against the metric tensor of the dual color gives the unit. [20] The unit tensor
is an identity for contraction at a slot, so raising and then lowering an index is a round
trip. [21] Raising or lowering a named index, by contraction with the metric, is an equivariant
linear equivalence. [22]

subsections.title: Evaluation
subsections.body:
One index of a tensor evaluates at a fixed basis label, on pure tensors and on tensors. [23]
Evaluation has explicit components in the basis, and commutes with permutations, with other
evaluations, with contractions and with products in their right factor. [23] A tensor is the sum
over basis labels of the evaluations of its last index, each tensored with the matching rank-one
basis tensor and permuted back into the last slot. [23] Evaluation also commutes with a product
in its left factor and with contraction in the opposite order, and two evaluations of the same
tensor commute. [TODO]

subsections.title: Constructing tensors
subsections.body:
Tensors arise from single vectors, from elements of a tensor product of two or three carriers,
and from invariant maps. [24] They also arise from integer components in the standard
basis. [25] Complex Lorentz tensors arise from Gaussian-integer components, compatibly with
products, contractions and permutations. [26]

subsections.title: Index notation
subsections.body:
An elaborator turns pen-and-paper index expressions into tensor operations. [27] The design follows
Tooby-Smith {1}. A class carries index notation to any type linearly equivalent to a tensor, with
the induced group action, basis and products. [28]

subsections.title: Conjugation
subsections.body:
A species may carry a conjugation: a second involution on colors together with a conjugation of
tensors, which is involutive and commutes with contraction. [29] A componentwise criterion for a
tensor to equal a permutation of its conjugate expresses reality, and gives the Hermitian
condition on a metric slot. [29] Both Lorentz species carry conjugations, so that reality and
Hermiticity conditions apply to real and complex Lorentz tensors. [TODO]

subsections.title: Real Lorentz tensors
subsections.body:
The real Lorentz tensors form a species over the Lorentz group {2} with an upper and a lower color,
each dual to the other; in it, contraction is a sum of evaluations. [30] Its colors are carried by
the contravariant and covariant modules, with their representations of the Lorentz group and their
standard bases. [31][32] The two modules contract invariantly against each other. [33] The species
has metric maps [34] and unit maps. [35] Its metric tensors have the Minkowski matrix as components
in the standard basis, and raising or lowering an index multiplies components by the Minkowski
matrix. [36] Its unit tensor has explicit components. [37] Pairwise tensor products of the two
modules are square matrices. [38] The metrics and units of this species are intertwining maps of the
vector and covector representations, with no preliminary constructions or auxiliary modules.
[TODO]

subsections.title: Lorentz vectors and covectors
subsections.body:
A Lorentz vector is a function on one time index and d space indices. [39] Lorentz vectors carry
module, norm and inner-product structures, a charted-space structure, a standard basis and
coordinate maps, a time component and a spatial part, and a model with corners under which they
form a manifold. [39] The Lorentz group acts on them by matrix-vector multiplication. [40] They
are tensorial, the induced action on the standard basis being the matrix action. [41] Lorentz
covectors carry the same structures [42], the same kind of representation [43], and a tensorial
instance. [44] Vectors and covectors contract invariantly against each other. [45]

subsections.title: Minkowski product and causality
subsections.body:
The Minkowski product of two Lorentz vectors is symmetric, Lorentz invariant and
nondegenerate. [46] Linear maps have adjoints with respect to it, and a linear map preserves it
exactly when its matrix lies in the Lorentz group. [46]

Each vector has a causal character — timelike, lightlike or spacelike — that is invariant under
Lorentz transformations, and the product determines light cones, causal precedence and causal
diamonds. [47] A vector is spacelike exactly when its Minkowski norm squared is negative. [47] It
is timelike exactly when that norm squared is positive, and then its time component dominates its
spatial part. [48] It is lightlike exactly when that norm squared vanishes, and causal precedence
is reflexive. [49] A Lorentz velocity is a future-directed vector of unit Minkowski norm; its time
component is positive and dominates its spatial part, and the velocities form a path-connected
set. [50]

subsections.title: Levi-Civita tensor
subsections.body:
The rank-four Levi-Civita tensor is a real Lorentz tensor in three spatial dimensions whose
components in the standard basis are the Levi-Civita symbol, and it is antisymmetric under each
adjacent transposition of indices. [51] The Euclidean Levi-Civita symbol satisfies the
epsilon-epsilon contraction identities summed over all four index slots, over the last three,
and over the last two. [52] At the level of tensors, contracting the Levi-Civita tensor with
itself over all four index pairs gives −24, and over the first three gives −6 times the unit
tensor of the lower color. [63][64][37] A Euclidean Levi-Civita tensor carries the
epsilon-epsilon contraction identities as identities between tensors. [TODO]

subsections.title: Complex Lorentz tensors
subsections.body:
The complex Lorentz tensors form a species over SL(2, ℂ) with the left- and right-handed Weyl colors
{3}, their duals, and the two Lorentz vector colors. [53] The vector colors are carried by complex
contravariant and covariant modules with their representations of SL(2, ℂ), which contract
invariantly against each other. [54][55] The metric tensors [56] and unit tensors [57] of each color
have several equivalent forms, including Gaussian-integer components, and the units are symmetric.
[58] Pairwise products of complex Lorentz vectors are square matrices. [59] The full contraction of
an antisymmetric tensor with a symmetric one equals its own negative. [60] The complex Levi-Civita
tensor has Gaussian-integer components. [61]

subsections.title: From real to complex tensors
subsections.body:
A canonical injective semilinear map takes real Lorentz tensors to complex ones, sending colors
and component labels to their complex counterparts. [62] It is equivariant for the complexified
Lorentz group and commutes with permutations, products, contractions and evaluations of
indices. [62]

nodes.title: Galilean group
nodes.abstract:
The Galilean group is the group of transformations relating the descriptions two observers give
of non-relativistic space and time. An element records a spatial rotation, a boost velocity, a
translation of space and a translation of time, in any spatial dimension; it acts on a pair of
an instant and a point by rotating and boosting first, then translating, and it contains the
Euclidean group, the orthogonal group, the rotations, the space translations and the time
translations as subgroups.

content.heading: Content (Alpha)
content.intro:
A Galilean transformation consists of four pieces of data: a rotation, a boost velocity, a
translation of space {1} and a translation of time {2}. [1]
The spatial dimension is arbitrary; nothing is special to three dimensions. [6]

Galilean transformations form a group, with the identity, the composite and the inverse computed
explicitly from the four pieces. [2] This group is a Lie group. [TODO]

The Galilean group acts on time and space together: an element sends a pair of an instant and a
point to the pair obtained by rotating and boosting the point, then translating both. [7]

The Galilean group is assembled from familiar subgroups, each of which includes into it. The
rotations include into the Galilean group, as do the elements of the full orthogonal group. [3]
The space translations include into the Galilean group. [4] The time translations include into
the Galilean group. [5] More generally, the Euclidean group of space, the transformations
combining a rotation and a translation of space, includes into the Galilean group. [8]

declarations.doc: A Galilean transformation in `d` spatial dimensions. The fields are, in order, the spatial orthogonal part, boost velocity, spatial translation, and time translation.
declarations.signature:
structure GalileanGroup (d : ℕ := 3) where
  rotation : Matrix.orthogonalGroup (Fin d) ℝ
  velocity : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)
  spaceTranslation : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)
  timeTranslation : Time
lemma one_rotation : (1 : GalileanGroup d).rotation = 1
lemma one_velocity : (1 : GalileanGroup d).velocity = 0
lemma one_spaceTranslation : (1 : GalileanGroup d).spaceTranslation = 0
lemma one_timeTranslation : (1 : GalileanGroup d).timeTranslation = 0

lemma mul_rotation (g h : GalileanGroup d) :
    (g * h).rotation = g.rotation * h.rotation

lemma mul_velocity (g h : GalileanGroup d) :
    (g * h).velocity = g.rotation • h.velocity + g.velocity

lemma mul_spaceTranslation (g h : GalileanGroup d) :
    (g * h).spaceTranslation =
      g.spaceTranslation + g.rotation • h.spaceTranslation + h.timeTranslation.val • g.velocity

lemma mul_timeTranslation (g h : GalileanGroup d) :
    (g * h).timeTranslation = g.timeTranslation + h.timeTranslation

lemma inv_rotation (g : GalileanGroup d) :
    g⁻¹.rotation = g.rotation⁻¹

declarations.doc: The inverse boost velocity formula.
declarations.signature:
lemma inv_velocity (g : GalileanGroup d) :
    g⁻¹.velocity = -(g.rotation⁻¹ • g.velocity)

lemma inv_spaceTranslation (g : GalileanGroup d) :
    g⁻¹.spaceTranslation =
      -(g.rotation⁻¹ • g.spaceTranslation) +
        g.timeTranslation.val • (g.rotation⁻¹ • g.velocity)

lemma inv_timeTranslation (g : GalileanGroup d) :
    g⁻¹.timeTranslation = -g.timeTranslation

nodes.title: Reference frame
nodes.abstract:
An observer describing motion needs a coordinate grid, and the grid is a choice rather than a
feature of space: two points of space determine a displacement, but a
displacement acquires numerical components only once axes have been picked, the observer need not
use the zero point space carries, and no instant of time is canonically zero.
A reference frame is that collection of choices, a time origin together with an origin and a set
of axes carried along through time. An inertial frame is one whose grid is not being pushed
around, the setting in which the familiar Newtonian statements about free motion hold, and a
vector quantity measured by an observer is a list of components read off that observer's axes,
whose lengths and angles are nevertheless taken from the underlying space.

subsections.title: Frames
subsections.body:
A reference frame records a time origin, together with an affine origin and a basis of displacements
of space {1} at each time. [1] Its time origin converts a real time coordinate into an instant of
time {2}. [14] A frame can be built from the trajectories of a collection of reference points,
provided those points form an affine basis at every time: one point serves as the origin, and the
displacements from it to the others serve as the basis. [2] The origin and basis of a frame built in
this way are exactly those points and displacements. [TODO]

A frame may induce the same inner product on coordinates at every time, in which case it
conserves its coordinate metric. [3] A frame may also have orthonormal axes at every time; such a
frame conserves its coordinate metric, and typeclass inference knows this. [4]

subsections.title: Inertial frames
subsections.body:
A frame is inertial when its origin moves with constant velocity and its axes are the same at
every time, both measured against the affine structure that space itself supplies. [5] This is a
restriction on the observer rather than on whatever is being observed. An inertial frame's origin
has a definite constant velocity. [6] Over any elapsed time the origin is displaced by that
elapsed time multiplied by this velocity. [TODO] An inertial frame conserves its coordinate
metric, and typeclass inference knows this. [7]

The relative motion of two inertial frames is the boost, rotation and translation carrying one to
the other, and it induces a transformation law on measured components. [TODO] A frame whose
axes are constant and whose origin moves with constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is
itself inertial. [TODO]

subsections.title: Measured vector quantities
subsections.body:
A vector quantity measured by an observer, a relative position, a velocity, an acceleration, a
force, a momentum, is a list of components read off that observer's axes. These components have
a carrier of their own, equivalent to the tuples of coordinates. [8] They add and scale
componentwise, inheriting the additive and scalar structure of their entries, regardless of which
quantity they stand for; the physical dimension, units and transformation law belong to whatever
supplies the quantity. [9] The components carry a topology, a continuous linear equivalence with
coordinate tuples, and finite dimensionality. [11]

Through the frame's basis at a given time, such components name a geometric displacement in
space, as a linear and as a continuous linear map. [10] Lengths and angles are geometric facts
about that displacement rather than about the numbers. For a frame that conserves its coordinate
metric, the components carry a norm and an inner product pulled back through the frame basis from
displacement space, so that a displacement keeps its length and its angles even when the axes are
skew or unequally scaled. [12] In an orthonormal frame these reduce to the familiar Euclidean
formulas: the sum of the squared components gives the squared length, and the sum of the
componentwise products gives the inner product. [13]

The derivative of a trajectory expressed in a frame gives the velocity and acceleration that frame
measures, as the time derivative of the coordinate components. [TODO]

nodes.title: Space
nodes.abstract:
A point of space is modelled by its d real coordinates, read against an arbitrary but fixed
choice of length unit and origin; the default dimension is three, but nothing is special to it,
and the space is flat and Euclidean throughout. Around that bare structure sit the structures
physics needs on space: a metric and a torsor over the Euclidean space of the same dimension, a
vector space once the origin is fixed, a norm and an inner product, and a smooth manifold,
together with a basis and coordinates, length units, the cross product in three dimensions, the
relation between spaces of different dimension, and the actions of translations and rotations.
Space is also the home of differentiation in a spatial direction, for functions and for
distributions, of gradient, divergence and curl, and of the distributions made from functions
that are bounded in the appropriate sense.

subsections.title: Points of space and their structure
subsections.body:
A point of space is given by its d real coordinates. [1] Space is a type of its own, distinct
from the Euclidean space of the same dimension although closely related to it, a choice discussed
on the Lean Zulip {1}.
Subtracting two points of space gives a vector of Euclidean space. [8] Space is a normed torsor
over Euclidean space of the same dimension. [9]

Space has a choice of origin, the zero of its vector space structure, and a standard
affine-isometry chart onto Euclidean space of the same dimension. [5] Once the origin is taken as
its zero, space is a real vector space. [2] It carries a norm, an inner product and a metric,
making it a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and a metric space. [3][4] It has basis
vectors, one for each coordinate direction, forming an orthonormal basis. [7]

Space is a smooth manifold, charted over Euclidean space of the same dimension through a
homeomorphism with it. [6]

subsections.title: Dimensions, units and the cross product
subsections.body:
Spaces of different dimensions are related: one dimension of space splits off as a real factor,
and one-dimensional space is isometrically the reals. [14][15] A choice of length unit rescales
lengths, and concrete units such as the metre are available. [16]

Three-dimensional Euclidean space carries the cross product. Taking the cross product with a fixed
vector commutes with the time derivative, and the cross product of a vector with another is
orthogonal to it. [17]

subsections.title: Translations and rotations
subsections.body:
Points of space can be translated, and so can distributions on space. [10][11] The group of
rotations acts on space, and that action agrees with multiplying coordinates by the rotation
matrix. [12][13]

subsections.title: Derivatives and distributions
subsections.body:
A function from space into a normed space can be differentiated along a coordinate
direction. [18] A function from space into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

A function bounded in the appropriate sense determines a distribution on space; the constant
function and the constant slice are such distributions. [19][20][21][22] A distribution on space
valued in a normed space can be differentiated, giving also its gradient, its divergence and its
curl. [23][24][25][26] A distribution from space into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

nodes.title: SpaceTime
nodes.abstract:
Minkowski space-time, for an arbitrary but fixed choice of units and origin and an arbitrary
spatial dimension, is a Lorentz vector: a point is its time and space coordinates taken together,
and the Lorentz group acts on it. Around it sit the coordinate maps, the projections onto space
and onto time and the equivalence with their product, the measure-space structure that
integration over space-time needs, including the splitting of such an integral into an integral
over time of an integral over space, differentiation along a coordinate for functions and for
distributions, and the slicing of either at a fixed instant.

subsections.title: Points of space-time
subsections.body:
A point of Minkowski space-time is a Lorentz vector {1} of coordinates, for an arbitrary but
fixed choice of units and origin. [1] Space-time maps onto space {2} and onto time {3}, and is
equivalent to their product. [2]

The Lorentz group {4} acts on space-time, and through it
on Schwartz maps and distributions on space-time. [8] A rotation about the coordinate origin acts
on space-time through the Lorentz group and on space through the Euclidean group, and the
spatial projection intertwines these two actions of one and the same special orthogonal
rotation. [3]

subsections.title: Integration and slicing
subsections.body:
Space-time carries the measure-space structure that integration over it uses: a Borel
measurable space with an additive Haar volume measure. [9] An integral over space-time splits
into an integral over space and an integral over time, in either order. [7] A function or a
distribution on space-time can be sliced at a fixed instant. [10]

subsections.title: Derivatives
subsections.body:
A function from space-time into a normed space can be differentiated along a coordinate, and its
derivatives assemble into a tensor. [4] A function from space-time into a manifold can be
differentiated along a coordinate too, giving a tangent vector at its value. [5] A distribution
on space-time valued in a normed space can be differentiated. [6] A distribution from space-time
into a manifold is differentiable. [TODO]

nodes.title: Time
nodes.abstract:
An instant of time is modelled by a single real number, read against an arbitrary but fixed
choice of unit and orientation, so that a statement about time has to hold whichever unit and
whichever direction of time is picked. Instants form an affine space over the reals with no
distinguished present moment; choosing the implicit origin turns it into the one-dimensional real
inner-product space that non-relativistic physics usually works with, carrying the norm, the inner
product, the order and the volume measure. On top of this sit the derivative of a function of
time, for targets that are normed spaces and for targets that are manifolds, time as a bare
oriented manifold, and the choices of time unit, from seconds up to weeks.

subsections.title: Instants and their structure
subsections.body:
An instant of time is a single real number, for an arbitrary but fixed choice of unit and
orientation. [1] Instants form an affine space over the reals: a real number translates an
instant to another instant, and any two instants differ by a real elapsed time. [2] No instant is
canonically zero.

Given the implicit origin, the instant whose real number is zero, time is a real vector space of
dimension one. It has an orthonormal basis and continuous linear and isometric equivalences to the
reals. [3] Instants are ordered, so that one instant comes no later than another. [4] Time carries
a norm, and an inner product making it a one-dimensional real inner-product space. [5] It is a
Borel measurable space whose volume measure is the Haar measure of the basis, and the
identification with the reals preserves that measure. [6] Time carries an action of the
translation group. [TODO]

Time with no structure beyond its orientation is a manifold in its own right, with its topology,
its charted-space and manifold structures, and a diffeomorphism to the reals. [10]

subsections.title: Derivatives in time
subsections.body:
A function from time into a normed space has a time derivative. The derivative is compatible with
scalar multiplication and with quotients, kills constants, and preserves smoothness. Differentiating
a function valued in Euclidean space, or in Lorentz vectors {1}, agrees with differentiating its
components one at a time. [7] The time derivative of a product of square-matrix-valued functions
obeys the product rule, and the time derivative commutes with the transpose. [9]

A function from time into a manifold has a time derivative too, and for a target that is both a
normed space and a manifold the two derivatives agree. [8]

Distributions from time into a normed space are differentiable. [TODO] Distributions from time
into a manifold are differentiable. [TODO]

subsections.title: Units of time
subsections.body:
A choice of time unit is a positive real number. Two units have a ratio, and a unit rescales an
elapsed time. The concrete units run from seconds up to weeks, with the relations between them,
such as the number of seconds in an hour. [11]

nodes.title: TimeAndSpace
nodes.abstract:
Euclidean space-time, the arena of non-relativistic physics, is an instant of time together with
a point of d-dimensional space, and nothing more: in the non-relativistic setting no symmetry the
theory respects mixes the two factors, so the product is the whole story. It has projections onto
the two factors that do not increase distances, an action of the Euclidean group on its points and
on the Schwartz maps out of it, and time and space derivatives that commute, together with the
characterisation of the functions that are constant in one of the two directions.

content.heading: Content (Alpha)
content.intro:
A point of Euclidean space-time is a pair of an instant of time {1} and a point of d-dimensional
space {2}. [1] Space-time projects onto its time and its space
factor, continuously and linearly, and each projection moves a pair of points no further apart
than they were. [2]

The Euclidean group of space acts on space-time, each element as an isometry which splits into a
linear part and a translation. [3] That action carries over to the Schwartz maps out of
space-time, where each element acts injectively and surjectively. [4]

Differentiating a function on space-time in time and differentiating it in space commute, and
the time derivative commutes with the curl. [5] A function on space-time whose time derivative
vanishes depends only on the point of space, one whose space derivative vanishes depends only on
the instant, and one with both vanishing is constant. [6]

nodes.title: Canonical ensemble
nodes.abstract:
A canonical ensemble describes a system in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at a fixed
temperature. Its data is
a measurable type of microstates, an energy function on them, and the semi-classical bookkeeping
(the number of degrees of freedom and the phase-space unit) needed to turn thermodynamic
quantities into dimensionless ones. The treatment is measure-theoretic, so that discrete and
continuous models are handled uniformly: the partition function is an integral, which becomes a
finite sum when the microstates are finitely many. On that footing the Boltzmann and probability
measures, the mean energy, the entropies and the Helmholtz free energy are tied together by the
free energy as energy minus temperature times entropy, the mean energy as a derivative of the
logarithm of the partition function, and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem relating the heat
capacity to the variance of the energy; ensembles also compose, with independent systems adding
and a system being copied or transported along a measurable equivalence.

subsections.title: Ensembles and their measures
subsections.body:
A canonical ensemble {1} is given by its microstates, its energy function, its degrees of freedom,
its phase-space unit and a σ-finite measure; independent ensembles add, a system has several
non-interacting copies, and an ensemble transports along a measurable equivalence. [1] The
temperature enters through the inverse temperature {2}. An ensemble carries an
unnormalized Boltzmann measure and a normalized probability measure, together with pointwise
mathematical and physical probability densities. [2] The mathematical partition function is the
integral of the Boltzmann factor, and the physical one is that divided by the phase-space unit
raised to the degrees of freedom; both are positive. [3]

subsections.title: Thermodynamic quantities
subsections.body:
An ensemble has a mean energy, a mean square energy and an energy variance, [4] and the
variance is the mean square minus the square of the mean. [5] The Helmholtz free energy comes
from the partition function. [6] An ensemble has a differential entropy and an absolute
thermodynamic entropy, [7] and for finitely many microstates the thermodynamic entropy is the
Shannon entropy. [8]

The fundamental thermodynamic identity holds: the free energy is the mean energy less the
temperature times the entropy. [9] The mean energy is minus the derivative of the logarithm of
the partition function with respect to the inverse temperature. [10] The heat capacity is the
derivative of the mean energy with respect to temperature, and whenever the energy variance is
minus the derivative of the mean energy with respect to the inverse temperature, the heat
capacity is the energy variance divided by the Boltzmann constant times the square of the
temperature. [11] For a finite ensemble at positive temperature this fluctuation–dissipation
theorem holds outright. [12] These identities are developed in Tong's lectures {3}.

subsections.title: Finite ensembles and the two-state system
subsections.body:
For systems with finitely many discrete microstates the integral definitions reduce to finite
sums. [13] The two-state ensemble has closed forms for its partition function, its state
probabilities and its mean energy. [14] Its thermodynamic entropy has a closed form. [TODO]
Its Helmholtz free energy has a closed form. [TODO]

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.abstract:
Temperature is measured from absolute zero and is nonnegative, which excludes the negative absolute
temperatures a system with a bounded energy spectrum can carry. A choice of scale is a choice of how
large one degree is, and nothing more, so two such choices differ by a positive ratio, and kelvin is
the scale from which the others are obtained by rescaling. In statistical mechanics the quantity
that actually appears is the inverse temperature, the reciprocal of the temperature weighted by the
Boltzmann constant, which multiplies an energy in a Boltzmann factor; on positive temperatures the
correspondence is an order-reversing bijection onto the positive inverse temperatures, so a hot
system is one with a small inverse temperature, and sending the inverse temperature to infinity
drives the temperature to absolute zero. Thermodynamic quantities are differentiated with respect to
one or the other of these variables, so the change of variable between them is smooth at positive
temperature, and a derivative in one variable determines the derivative in the other.

subsections.title: Absolute temperature and inverse temperature
subsections.body:
An absolute temperature is a nonnegative real in an arbitrary scale that puts absolute zero at zero;
it coerces to the nonnegative reals and to the reals, carries a topology and a zero, and is
determined by its value. [1] This excludes the negative absolute temperatures that a system with a
bounded energy spectrum can carry {1}. A temperature is built from a nonnegative real, or from a
real together with a proof that it is nonnegative. [7] The temperature enters the Gibbs distribution
through its inverse {2}. A temperature has an inverse temperature, formed with the Boltzmann
constant [14], and a temperature is recovered from an inverse temperature. [2] Passing to the inverse
temperature and back is the identity, in both directions. [3] A strictly positive temperature has a
strictly positive inverse temperature. [4] The boundary value zero is paired with itself, which is a
convention of the underlying nonnegative reals rather than a physical statement.

The temperature is a continuous function of the inverse temperature at positive inverse
temperature, and its real coordinate is differentiable on the positive reals. [5] In the limit
of large inverse temperature the temperature is eventually positive and converges to absolute
zero from above, the regime in which a system settles into its lowest energy states. [6] At
positive temperature the inverse temperature has a derivative with respect to the temperature,
and the chain rule converts a derivative in one variable into a derivative in the other. [8]

subsections.title: Temperature scales
subsections.body:
A temperature unit is a choice of scale, carrying a positive scale factor. [9][10] Two
temperature units have a ratio, a nonnegative real, which is positive and behaves reflexively,
symmetrically and multiplicatively along a chain of units. [11] A temperature unit rescales by a
positive real, with the ratios this induces and its composition law. [12] Kelvin is the reference
temperature unit, and the other units, among them the nanokelvin, microkelvin, millikelvin and
the absolute Fahrenheit-sized degree, are obtained from it by rescaling. [13]

The temperature manifold is diffeomorphic to the nonnegative reals, and a temperature unit is a
translationally invariant metric on it. [TODO] A temperature value converts between two
temperature units. [TODO] Degrees Celsius and degrees Fahrenheit, as ordinarily used, are
scales whose zero is offset from absolute zero, and they convert to absolute scales. [TODO]

nodes.title: Units
nodes.abstract:
Every physical quantity has a dimension: a rational power of each base dimension, recording how
the numerical value of the quantity changes when the unit of each base quantity is changed.
Dimensions multiply by adding exponents and invert by negating them, so they form a commutative
group with a rational power operation. Two sets of base dimensions are in use: the LTMCT set of
length, time, mass, charge and temperature, over which the typed unit layer and the named
derived quantities are built, and the seven base quantities of the International System of
Quantities (ISQ), in which charge is derived as current times time; the two are related by a
faithful inclusion and a reduction. A unit system fixes one unit for each base quantity, and
changing unit system multiplies a quantity of dimension d by a positive factor that is
multiplicative in d, equal to one when the two systems agree and composes along a chain, so the
value of a quantity in one system determines its value in every other. A value carrying a
dimension inherits the additive, order and scalar structure of its underlying type, and a
statement is dimensionally correct when its truth does not depend on the unit system in which it
is written, which is the formal content of dimensional analysis.

subsections.title: Dimensions
subsections.body:
A dimension assigns a rational exponent to each base dimension, and two dimensions with the same
exponents are equal. [1] Dimensions form a commutative group with a rational power operation.
[2] The exponents of a product, of the unit, of an inverse, of a quotient and of a natural power
follow from the exponents of the factors. [3] Each base dimension has its base vector, whose
exponents are one at that base dimension and zero elsewhere. [4] The vocabulary of base
quantity, derived quantity and quantity dimension is that of ISO/IEC 80000-1 {1} and of the
International vocabulary of metrology {2}. The design of this API is discussed on the Lean
Zulip {3}.

A change of base-dimension set is a monoid homomorphism of dimensions, either an injective
embedding of one set into another or a surjective reduction of a richer set onto a coarser one,
so a relabelling that does not preserve products, inverses and rational powers is not
expressible. [5]

subsections.title: The LTMCT and ISQ base sets
subsections.body:
The LTMCT set has five base dimensions, length, time, mass, charge and temperature, whose
initials give the name, each with its exponent projection. [6] A dimension over this set is
built from its five exponents. [7] Each of the five exponents of a product, a unit, an inverse,
a quotient and a natural power follows from those of the factors. [8] The generators L𝓭, T𝓭,
M𝓭, C𝓭 and Θ𝓭 are the base vectors of the five base dimensions. [9]

The International System of Quantities has seven base quantities. [10] In it electric charge is
derived as current times time, with exponent one in current and in time and zero in mass. [11]
Amount of substance and luminous intensity are base dimensions of their own, distinct from the
trivial dimension. [12]

A faithful embedding carries the LTMCT base dimensions into the ISQ set, sending the charge
generator to the derived ISQ charge. [13] A reduction runs the other way, reading electric
current as charge per time and forgetting amount of substance and luminous intensity. [14] The
reduction is a retraction of the embedding, and the composite in the other order is not the
identity. [15]

subsections.title: Unit choices and the change of unit
subsections.body:
A unit choice fixes one unit for each of the five LTMCT base quantities, with the SI choice of
metre, second, kilogram, coulomb and kelvin. [16] The SI unit choice over the five LTMCT base
quantities is computable, its base units being given without axioms. [TODO] A second unit
choice rescales each SI base unit by a distinct prime, which serves to refute dimensional
correctness. [17]

The factor by which a quantity of a given dimension rescales under a change of unit choice is a
monoid homomorphism from dimensions to the positive reals. [18] It is one on the trivial
dimension and on a unit system paired with itself. [19] It is strictly positive and nonzero,
composes along a chain of three unit choices, and inverts when the two choices are swapped. [20]
Scaling by it is injective. [21] This is the classical law for the change of a quantity under a
change of unit {4}.

subsections.title: Unit systems over a general base set
subsections.body:
The change-of-unit law holds once for a general set of base dimensions and specialises to the
LTMCT set and to the ISQ set without being restated. A magnitude layer assigns a positive real
to each base dimension, with nonzero ratios. [26] On it the scaling homomorphism is the product
over the base dimensions of the unit ratio raised to the corresponding exponent, and it is
transitive. [27] A catalogue names a type of admissible units and a magnitude for each base
dimension, and a unit system chooses exactly one unit per base dimension. [28] A unit system
projects onto the magnitude layer. [29] The five-field LTMCT unit choice is equivalent to a unit
system over the LTMCT base dimensions, and its scaling law is the generic product specialised to
that set. [30][31]

Units of electric current, of amount of substance and of luminous intensity are each a positive
magnitude, with a quotient by another unit of the same kind. [32][33] The coherent SI units are
the ampere, the mole and the candela. [34] These unit types carry the same rescaling operation
as the other five, so that a decimal multiple such as the milliampere exists. [37][38] A unit
choice over the seven ISQ base quantities fixes one unit for each, with the coherent SI choice
of metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. [35] Its scaling factor is the
generic product over the ISQ base quantities. [36] The SI base units are those of the SI
Brochure {5}.

subsections.title: Dimension-carrying and unit-dependent types
subsections.body:
A type may carry a dimension, and the stronger notion is a type carrying a dimension on which
the positive reals act. [22] A function from unit choices to a dimension-carrying type has a
dimension when it rescales by the factor of that dimension under every change of unit. [23] The
functions with this property form a subtype carrying a scalar action. [24] For each fixed unit
choice, a value of a dimension-carrying type is equivalent to a quantity given in every unit
system. [25]

A unit-dependent type comes with a transformation of its elements under a change of unit, which
composes along a chain of unit choices and is trivial on an unchanged choice. [39] Stronger
versions require that transformation to commute with a scalar action, to be linear, or to be
linear and continuous. [40] The transformation is then an equivalence, a linear map, a linear
equivalence, a continuous linear map or a continuous linear equivalence. [41] The unit choices
themselves and every dimension-carrying type are unit-dependent. [42] Function types are
unit-dependent, with the transformation acting on the argument, on the value, or on both. [43]

A quantity or a statement is dimensionally correct when it is unchanged by a change of unit
system; for functions this unfolds into conditions acting on the argument, on the value and on
both. [44] The dimension-preserving product of two dimension-carrying types scales as the
product of their dimensions. [45] The elements of a unit-dependent type that scale according to
a prescribed dimension form a subset which itself carries that dimension. [46]

subsections.title: Dimension-tagged values
subsections.body:
Values of an underlying type may be tagged with a dimension over any set of base dimensions.
[47] The tagged type inherits zero, addition, negation and subtraction, each computed on the
underlying value. [48] It inherits the order relations and the action of the positive reals.
[49] Multiplying or dividing real-valued tagged quantities multiplies or divides the underlying
values and combines the dimensions in the same way. [50] Over the LTMCT base dimensions a tagged
type carries its dimension, and its transformation under a change of unit is scalar
multiplication by the scaling factor. [51] A tagged quantity of trivial dimension is unchanged
by a change of unit. [52] A cast moves a tagged quantity between two tags whose dimensions are
equal, with the equality discharged automatically. [53]

At a fixed numerical unit representation, tagged values form a real module without replacing the
existing additive operations or the action of the nonnegative reals. [68] They also form a
normed space, and explicit coordinate equivalences transport functions and their Fréchet
derivatives. [69] The tagged type inherits further structure from its underlying type:
multiplicative and other non-additive algebraic structure, the rest of the order structure, and
topological structure. [TODO]

subsections.title: Named quantities
subsections.body:
The base quantities themselves are the subject of the APIs for time {6}, space {7} and
temperature {8}, and of the mass and charge modules.
Area has dimension length squared, with the square metre, square foot, square mile, are, hectare
and acre, their values in SI units, and one acre equal to 43560 square feet. [54] Speed has
dimension length over time, with the metre per second, mile per hour, kilometre per hour, knot
and the speed of light, their values in SI units, and the conversions between them. [55] Energy
has dimension mass times length squared over time squared, with the joule, electronvolt, calorie
and kilowatt hour. [56] Pressure has dimension mass over length over time squared, with the
pascal, millimetre of mercury, bar, standard atmosphere, torr and pound per square inch. [57]
Momentum has dimension mass times length over time and takes values in d spatial components:
it is the three-momentum rather than the four-momentum. [58] The mass of a particle is a named
dimension-carrying quantity in the manner of momentum, and so is its velocity in d spatial
dimensions. [TODO]

subsections.title: Calculus and dimensional correctness
subsections.body:
The derivative of a dimensionally correct differentiable function is dimensionally correct, and
the derivative at a rescaled point is the explicitly rescaled derivative. [59] The equation
giving the derivative in a fixed direction as a quantity of the dimension of the target divided
by the dimension of the source is dimensionally correct. [60] A measure on a dimension-carrying
type is unit-dependent, and the integral of a function whose dimension is that of its values
divided by the dimension of the measure has the dimension of the values. [61]

subsections.title: Examples
subsections.body:
A length of 400 metres converts to miles. [62] The relations E = m c^2 and F = m a, stated over
dimension-tagged reals, are dimensionally correct. [63] A speed as distance over time, an
expression of mixed dimension in mass, temperature, current, length and time, and the cosine of
an angular frequency times a time are each dimensionally correct. [64] The relation E = m c is
not dimensionally correct: a change of unit breaks it. [65] The version of E = m c^2 written with
the speed of light in an explicit unit system holds in SI units and, by transport, in every unit
system. [66]

The equality of a length with a speed times a time holds propositionally rather than
definitionally, so the two tagged types are bridged by a cast, and the same comparison works
over a set of base dimensions with no physical unit system, namely bits and symbols. [67]

The harmonic oscillator carries its mass and spring constant with their physical dimensions.
Its potential energy is assembled from dimension-tagged quantities, agrees in coordinates with
the numerical oscillator, and has its derivative from the generic transport of derivatives.
[70]

declarations.doc: A dimension over a represented basis `B`. PhysLib's default basis is `LTMCTDimensionBase`.
declarations.signature:
structure Dimension (B : Type) [DimensionBasis B] where
  exponents : DimensionBasis.Exponents B
lemma ext {d1 d2 : Dimension B} (h : ∀ b, d1.exponent b = d2.exponent b) : d1 = d2

lemma qpow_exponent (d : Dimension B) (q : ℚ) (b : B) :
    (d ^ q).exponent b = d.exponent b * Exponent.ofRat q

lemma mul_exponent (d1 d2 : Dimension B) (b : B) :
    (d1 * d2).exponent b = d1.exponent b + d2.exponent b
lemma one_exponent (b : B) : (1 : Dimension B).exponent b = 0
lemma inv_exponent (d : Dimension B) (b : B) : d⁻¹.exponent b = -d.exponent b

lemma div_exponent (d1 d2 : Dimension B) (b : B) :
    (d1 / d2).exponent b = d1.exponent b - d2.exponent b

lemma npow_exponent (d : Dimension B) (n : ℕ) (b : B) :
    (d ^ n).exponent b = n • d.exponent b

declarations.doc: The base-dimension vector for `b : B`: exponent `1` at `b`, `0` elsewhere. This is the generic analogue of the named generators `L𝓭`, `T𝓭`, …
declarations.signature: def single [DecidableEq B] (b : B) : Dimension B

lemma single_exponent [DecidableEq B] (b b' : B) :
    (single b).exponent b' = if b' = b then 1 else 0

declarations.doc: Change of basis along a map `f : B → B'` of base dimensions: reindex a dimension over `B` into one over `B'` by placing each exponent at its image. For an embedding `f` (injective) this preserves every exponent (`extend_exponent_apply`), so a dimension in one system re-expresses faithfully in an extending one.
declarations.signature:
def extend {B' : Type} [DimensionBasis B'] [Fintype B] [DecidableEq B']
    (f : B → B') (d : Dimension B) : Dimension B'

lemma extend_exponent_apply {B' : Type} [DimensionBasis B'] [Fintype B] [DecidableEq B']
    {f : B → B'} (hf : Function.Injective f) (d : Dimension B) (b : B) :
    (extend f d).exponent (f b) = d.exponent b

declarations.doc: `extend f` packaged as a monoid homomorphism of dimensions.
declarations.signature:
def extendHom {B' : Type} [DimensionBasis B'] [Fintype B] [DecidableEq B'] (f : B → B') :
    Dimension B →* Dimension B' where

declarations.doc: A **dimension embedding** `B ↪ B'`: an injective monoid homomorphism of dimensions. As a `MonoidHom` it is dimension-preserving (it respects products, inverses and rational powers); injectivity makes it a faithful inclusion of the basis `B` into `B'`. Cross-basis dimension injections are produced as `Embedding`s so that dimension-preservation holds by construction.
declarations.signature:
structure Embedding (B B' : Type) [DimensionBasis B] [DimensionBasis B'] where
  toHom : Dimension B →* Dimension B'
  inj : Function.Injective toHom

declarations.doc: A **dimension projection** `B' ↠ B`: a surjective monoid homomorphism of dimensions. As a `MonoidHom` it is truth-preserving, but it is lossy — it reduces a richer basis `B'` onto a coarser basis `B`, collapsing the base dimensions that `B` does not track.
declarations.signature:
structure Projection (B' B : Type) [DimensionBasis B'] [DimensionBasis B] where
  toHom : Dimension B' →* Dimension B
  surj : Function.Surjective toHom

declarations.doc: An injective *basis* map `f : B → B'` induces a dimension embedding, via `extend`. This is the label-level case: it sends each base dimension of `B` to a base dimension of `B'`, so it is automatically dimension-preserving and faithful.
declarations.signature:
def Embedding.ofBasis {B B' : Type} [DimensionBasis B] [DimensionBasis B']
    [Fintype B] [DecidableEq B']
    (f : B → B') (hf : Function.Injective f) : Embedding B B' where

    dimScale u1 u2 d * dimScale u2 u1 d = 1

structure WithDim {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] (d : Dimension B) (M : Type) where
  val : M

lemma dim_apply (d : Dimension LTMCTDimensionBase) (M : Type) :
    dim (WithDim d M) = d

lemma val_zero {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [Zero M] :
    (0 : WithDim d M).val = 0

lemma val_add {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [Add M]
    (m1 m2 : WithDim d M) :
    (m1 + m2).val = m1.val + m2.val

lemma val_neg {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [Neg M]
    (m : WithDim d M) :
    (-m).val = -m.val

lemma val_sub {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [Sub M]
    (m1 m2 : WithDim d M) :
    (m1 - m2).val = m1.val - m2.val

lemma le_def {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [LE M]
    (m1 m2 : WithDim d M) :
    m1 ≤ m2 ↔ m1.val ≤ m2.val

lemma lt_def {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [LT M]
    (m1 m2 : WithDim d M) :
    m1 < m2 ↔ m1.val < m2.val

lemma smul_val {B : Type} [DimensionBasis B] {d : Dimension B} {M : Type} [MulAction ℝ≥0 M]
    (a : ℝ≥0) (m : WithDim d M) :
